name: Beef, salt and water diet

card.summary: The most restrictive carnivore variant, popularised as the lion diet: ruminant meat, salt and water only, with no controlled evidence behind it.
card.note: Supported mainly by self-reports; dietitians' bodies classify carnivore diets as fad diets and flag nutrient gaps.

quick.overview:
This is a strict elimination-style version of the carnivore diet in which a person eats only beef or other ruminant meat, salt and water. It is often called the lion diet. It became widely known through Mikhaila Peterson and her father Jordan Peterson, who described following it.

Proponents describe it as a way to identify food sensitivities and to relieve autoimmune and mood symptoms. These accounts are anecdotal; no controlled trial has tested the diet.
quick.mechanism: Advocates say removing all plant foods and most other animal foods eliminates potential triggers such as plant compounds. Near-zero carbohydrate intake means the body relies on fat and protein for energy, usually in ketosis.
quick.risks: Critics cite missing fibre and micronutrients, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation and, with high red-meat intake, associations with colon cancer and gout. Grokipedia notes that early fatigue and cramps usually fade within weeks and that scurvy has been documented in a meat-only case.

lead: The beef, salt and water diet is the strictest form of the carnivore diet: nothing is eaten except ruminant meat (mostly beef), salt and water.[1][2] It is widely called the lion diet. People who follow it do so as an elimination protocol, aiming to find out which foods trigger skin flare-ups, bloating, joint pain or low mood, and many hope that a calmer system shows up as clearer skin, less facial puffiness and a leaner, more muscular physique.[2][3]

The diet reached a mass audience through Mikhaila Peterson, who began promoting a meat-only regimen around 2018 after describing childhood-onset arthritis and later depression, and her father Jordan Peterson, who moved to beef, salt and water in mid-2018.[1][3][11] It later spread through podcasts, YouTube, Instagram and TikTok.[1][2] Because beef is dense in protein, it is also used by some lifters and physique-focused dieters who want high protein intake with very few ingredients; a meat-only log on T Nation, for example, tracks bodyweight and training through a carnivore run.[6]

Research on the diet itself consists of self-reports. A 2021 survey of 2,029 long-term carnivore dieters, recruited through social media, found high satisfaction and few reported adverse symptoms, alongside sharply raised LDL cholesterol in the subset with lab values; its authors noted that the findings may not generalise.[8] A 2026 scoping review located only nine human studies of carnivore eating and described the evidence as very limited.[9] No randomised trial has tested a beef, salt and water regimen.[1][2] Dietetic organisations such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify carnivore eating as a fad diet and point to fibre and micronutrient gaps.[1]

chain: Only beef, salt and water are eaten
Common trigger foods are removed and protein stays high
Practitioners report calmer skin, less bloating and a leaner physique
angle.text: Followers use the diet as a strict reset: by removing every food other than beef they hope to identify what drives skin irritation, bloating or inflammation, and they report a leaner, less puffy look as a result. Its very high protein content also appeals to people building muscle. These outcomes are described by practitioners rather than measured in trials.

paras: The diet is a minimalist subset of the carnivore diet, which allows only animal products and excludes plants.[1] In its strict form it contains ruminant meat, salt and water and nothing else, and proponents present it as an elimination protocol to identify sensitivities.[2] Looser versions add poultry, fish, eggs or low-lactose dairy.[2] Carnivore variants are often described as high-protein, high-fat and near zero-carbohydrate.[1]

Ruminant meat is the defining ingredient. Grokipedia describes grass-fed beef or lamb as the base of the lion diet, with beef as the staple and fattier cuts preferred, since lean meat alone has long been reported to be poorly tolerated; Stefansson's 1920s observers made the same point.[2][12] The elimination logic is that, after a period on the minimal list, foods are reintroduced one at a time to see which provoke symptoms.[2] Followers sometimes describe the first weeks as an adjustment with fatigue, cramps and headaches, which Grokipedia links to electrolyte loss and says usually fades within weeks.[2]

The diet sits in a family of related eating patterns. Wikipedia notes later variants such as Paul Saladino's animal-based approach, which adds fruit, honey and raw dairy, and a 'carnivore traditionalism' emphasising pasture-raised beef and eggs.[1] Beef organ eating, discussed separately on appearance forums, is related but not the same as the strict lion diet.[5]

People who follow the diet for their looks usually cite three aims. The first is skin: followers report fewer breakouts, less redness and less irritation once plant foods and other common triggers are removed, which is the central promise of the elimination approach.[2] The second is body composition: a meat-only intake is high in protein, and trials comparing whole-food omnivorous and vegan meals have found higher muscle protein synthesis after the omnivorous meal in older adults, a finding carnivore advocates point to when describing animal protein as anabolic.[4] The third is facial leanness, which dieters link to reduced bloating and water retention, an effect reported anecdotally rather than measured.[6]

Weight loss is the most visible reported change. Grokipedia says Jordan Peterson reported a 52-pound loss over his years on the diet, and the 2021 survey recorded a lower median body mass index among respondents than before they started, according to its authors.[2][8] Reported body-composition changes in that survey came from the respondents themselves and were not verified by measurement.[8]

Earlier meat-heavy regimens include the 1856 book of Bernard Moncriff, the 1870s diabetes diets of Arnaldo Cantani and James H. Salisbury's 1880s lean beef and hot water diet, in which patients ate two to four pounds of lean beef a day with hot water.[1] Grokipedia also points to John Rollo's 1797 diabetes case reports and to Vilhjalmur Stefansson's medically observed meat-only year at Bellevue Hospital in 1928 and 1929 as historical reference points.[2]

Wikipedia's account of Stefansson says he and fellow explorer Karsten Anderson agreed to be observed at intervals at Bellevue, that the American Meat Institute is reported to have funded the study, and that the 1929 findings described a diet moderately high in protein and very high in fat, a mild prolonged ketosis, and poor tolerance of lean meat alone. The study's authors did not recommend the diet for general use.[12]

The modern carnivore diet drew attention in 2017 and 2018. Grokipedia dates its popularity to former orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker's 2017 appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience and his 2019 book, and to Jordan Peterson's 2018 discussion on the same podcast; Wikipedia places Baker's social-media promotion and the Petersons' lion diet in 2018.[1][2] Grokipedia says Mikhaila Peterson began a strict carnivore protocol in December 2017 and began promoting it in 2018.[2] Wikipedia's biography states that she was diagnosed with arthritis at age two, had hip and ankle replacements at 17, and experienced depression in adolescence; in 2018 she began sharing the diet through Instagram and a blog called Don't Eat That, followed by liondiet.com.[3] A 2018 caption crediting 'beef, salt, water and bourbon' for her recovery drew wide notice.[3]

Jordan Peterson's own account is summarised in his Wikipedia biography: in 2016 he limited his diet to meat and a few vegetables, partly to manage depression and symptoms of an autoimmune disorder, and by mid-2018 he ate only beef, salt and water.[11] Grokipedia reports that by 2024 he said he had followed it for seven years.[2] The same biography records his later health crisis in 2019 and 2020, involving benzodiazepine dependence and treatment abroad; it does not itself attribute that episode to the diet, and he has linked his drug use to family illness.[11]

A 2023 comment from neurologist Steven Novella, cited by Wikipedia, called carnivore eating the latest fad diet and noted its high cost.[1] Wikipedia's article on Mikhaila Peterson records that her blog was criticised after a Joe Rogan appearance, that The Guardian reported on her brief private consultations, and that she later launched further ventures in health and science media, including a 2023 mold-related research site.[3]

Advocates claim relief of autoimmune, digestive, skin and mood problems, attributing this to removal of plant compounds such as lectins and oxalates; Grokipedia describes these claims as largely anecdotal.[2] Proponents also describe ketosis, lower insulin and reduced inflammation as mechanisms, which Grokipedia characterises as theoretical rather than confirmed by long-term trials.[2]

The most-cited data point is the 2021 survey by Lennerz and colleagues, an online social-media survey run from March to June 2020 among adults who had eaten a carnivore diet for at least six months. Of 2,029 respondents, 67 percent were men, the median age was 44, and the median time on the diet was 14 months. Most ate red meat daily, and fewer than 10 percent ate vegetables, fruit or grains more than monthly. Respondents reported high satisfaction, improved health and well-being, few adverse symptoms, and, among those with diabetes, lower HbA1c and medication use.[8] In the subset with lipid results, LDL cholesterol was markedly elevated while HDL and triglycerides were in the optimal range.[8] Grokipedia stresses that the sample was self-selected and unvalidated, with no control group.[2][8]

A small 2025 German study of 24 carnivore dieters found that most blood values stayed within reference ranges, that total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol rose significantly, and that two participants with pre-diabetic HbA1c and six with elevated triglycerides saw those values fall.[10]

Nutrition professionals describe the carnivore diet as a fad diet; the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia are among bodies that classify it that way.[1] Cited concerns include lack of dietary fibre, vitamin deficiencies from excluding fruit and vegetables, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, and links between high red-meat intake and colon cancer, gout and kidney strain.[1]

Grokipedia lists possible shortfalls of vitamin C, folate, magnesium, potassium, calcium, thiamin and iodine, noting that beef alone is low in iodine, and describes a scurvy case in a man eating mostly canned beef whose symptoms returned when he resumed the diet. It also describes protein toxicity ('rabbit starvation') with very lean meat and two patients with LDL above 500 mg/dL whose levels improved when carbohydrates were reintroduced.[2]

A 2026 scoping review of nine human studies reported possible short-term benefits such as weight loss, satiety and changes in inflammatory or metabolic markers, together with deficiencies in vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre, and higher LDL and total cholesterol. Its authors judged the evidence very limited, citing small samples, short durations and no control groups, and did not recommend long-term adherence.[9]

Because the beef, salt and water version excludes eggs, dairy and organ meat, its nutrient profile is narrower than other carnivore variants; Grokipedia notes that organ meats, dairy, seafood, eggs and iodised salt are the foods usually suggested to narrow gaps in the broader carnivore diet.[2] Critics also raise environmental and cost concerns about meat-only eating.[1]

Meat-only eating is discussed on T Nation by lifters who log carnivore runs with bodyweight and training notes.[6] In one thread, a poster describes beef, salt and water as 'a form of an elimination diet' when advising another member on restarting from simple foods.[7] On looksmax.org, beef organs such as liver are promoted in long threads as nutrient-dense foods, a related but separate practice from the strict lion diet.[5]

Beyond forums, the diet circulates through social media creators. Grokipedia says female 'meatfluencers' on TikTok and YouTube had broadened the diet's audience by 2024.[2] Wikipedia also records that a far-right influencer, Raw Egg Nationalist, promoted a raw-food animal-based variant; the diet's political and cultural associations are part of how it is covered in media.[1]

No studies found. No controlled trial has tested a beef, salt and water diet. Related evidence for the wider carnivore diet consists of a 2021 self-selected survey of 2,029 adults, a 2025 explorative study of 24 German carnivore dieters, case reports, and a 2026 scoping review that located nine human studies.[8][10][9][2] Separate randomised work on protein sources, such as a 2024 trial in older adults comparing omnivorous and vegan meals, measured muscle protein synthesis rather than carnivore eating.[4]

timeline.event: John Rollo's diabetes case reports describe animal-food diets, per Grokipedia.[2]
Bernard Moncriff's book promotes an exclusively animal diet.[1]
James H. Salisbury promotes a lean beef and hot water diet.[1]
Vilhjalmur Stefansson and Karsten Anderson begin a year of meat-only eating under observation at Bellevue Hospital; results are published in 1929.[2][12]
Jordan Peterson limits his diet to meat and a few vegetables.[11]
Mikhaila Peterson develops the lion diet as an elimination protocol; Shawn Baker appears on The Joe Rogan Experience (per Grokipedia).[2]
Mikhaila Peterson shares the diet publicly; Jordan Peterson moves to beef, salt and water by mid-year.[1][3][11]
Shawn Baker publishes The Carnivore Diet (per Grokipedia).[2]
Lennerz and colleagues publish a survey of 2,029 carnivore dieters in Current Developments in Nutrition.[8]
Neurologist Steven Novella calls the carnivore diet the latest fad diet.[1]
An explorative study of 24 German carnivore dieters reports raised LDL cholesterol in the group.[10]
A scoping review of nine human carnivore-diet studies is published in Nutrients.[9]

lore.intro: Communities describe the diet as an elimination protocol, an extreme carnivore challenge and, among lifters, a simple high-protein structure.[2][6][7]

claims.claim: Eating only beef, salt and water resolves autoimmune and mood problems.
claims.believers: Proponents, led by Mikhaila Peterson, say removing everything but ruminant meat identifies trigger foods and relieves arthritis and depression.[2][3]
claims.experts: Grokipedia describes the evidence as largely anecdotal, with no large randomised trials, and dietetic bodies classify carnivore diets as fad diets.[1][2]

claims.claim: A meat-only diet clears skin and leans out the face and body.
claims.believers: Followers report fewer breakouts and a less puffy look after dropping plant foods and dairy, and lifters report keeping muscle while cutting.[6]
claims.experts: No published trial has measured skin or facial changes on this diet; research on protein and muscle concerns protein sources in general.[4]

claims.claim: Humans do not need plant foods.
claims.believers: Advocates point to traditional animal-heavy diets such as those of the Inuit, Maasai and Plains peoples.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes Inuit diets differ in organ content, seafood and raw meat and included gathered plants; critics cite missing fibre and micronutrients and a documented scurvy case.[1][2]

claims.claim: It lowers inflammation and improves metabolic health through ketosis.
claims.believers: Proponents describe lower insulin, ketone fuel use and reduced inflammation, and survey respondents with diabetes reported lower HbA1c and medication use.[2][8]
claims.experts: The survey authors note limits on generalising self-reports, and the 2026 scoping review describes the evidence as very limited and flags higher LDL and total cholesterol.[8][9]

claims.claim: Dropping lectins and oxalates is what makes the diet work.
claims.believers: Advocates say plant compounds such as lectins, oxalates and phytates irritate the gut and drive symptoms.[2]
claims.experts: Grokipedia describes these mechanisms as largely theoretical and unproven by long-term trials.[2]

claims.claim: The high LDL seen on the diet is harmless.
claims.believers: The 2021 survey found HDL and triglycerides in the optimal range, which supporters cite alongside high LDL.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and the German explorative study report raised LDL and total cholesterol, which the authors flag for further study; Wikipedia links LDL to cardiovascular risk.[1][10]

claims.claim: Meat-only eating builds muscle and a lean physique.
claims.believers: Lifters log bodyweight and training through carnivore runs and describe beef as a simple high-protein base.[6]
claims.experts: A 2024 trial found higher muscle protein synthesis after an omnivorous than a vegan meal in older adults; no trial has tested beef, salt and water specifically.[4]
